newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Weak Australia jobs data boost rate cut hope.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Weak Australia jobs data boost rate cut hope.

text.p: Australia's labour market remained weak in June with official data on Thursday showing unemployment fell in the month but mostly due to people apparently abandoning the search for work.

Economists said the data showing a smaller-than-expected rise of 11,900 in the total number of employed people in June and the headline unemployment rate down to 8.5 percent from 8.8 percent in May boosted expectations for another rate cut.
The increase in employment was well below median market forecasts of a 40,000 rise and masked a fall of 16,900 in the number of people in full-time work.
The Australian dollar slipped and bond futures firmed on a feeling that the soft data would put pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to cut official interest rates again.

The dollar fell to US$0.7410/15 from US$0.7439/44 shortly after the jobs data was released at 0130 GMT while the September 10-year bond futures contract went to 93.340 against a pre-data 93.285. Bill futures also firmed.
The RBA has cut the official cash rate four times in the past year, each time by half a percentage point. The last cut, on May 23, took it down to 5.5 percent.
But the rate cuts have yet to create a feel-good effect flowing through fully to consumer and business confidence.
Economists said the figures, and especially the drop in full-time employment, increased the likelihood of another rate cut in coming weeks to at least 60 percent.
Bill Evans, chief economist at Westpac Banking Corp, said the data was weaker than indicated by the headline unemployment rate. "So it leaves the way open for another rate cut," Evans added.
UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said: "It is a very, very weak result. Total employment for the first half of this year is fractionally lower than where it was at the end of December."

"Given that we have got inflation data coming up in a couple of weeks and that looks very, very benign, the issue is when are they (the RBA) going to ease, and I think that you keep watching the screens," Roberts said.
